article.overview: A gamma-ray detector measures high-energy photons, called gamma rays, that are emitted when natural radioactive isotopes decay in the lunar ground and when cosmic rays trigger nuclear reactions in the surface material. Each element emits gamma rays at characteristic energies, so the energy spectrum recorded by the detector can be used to identify the elements present and estimate their abundances [2][4]. Lunar gamma-ray spectrometers have so far been flown mainly in lunar orbit, where they map the composition of the surface beneath the spacecraft [2][4][6].
article.description: In practice a lunar gamma-ray detector is a spectrometer. The Lunar Prospector instrument combined a bismuth germanate (BGO) crystal with a borated-plastic anticoincidence shield. Events that trigger only the main crystal are accepted, and events that trigger both the crystal and the shield are rejected [1][2]. The Kaguya instrument used a large germanium crystal, which gives much finer energy resolution, together with a BGO and plastic anticoincidence system; the germanium crystal must be cooled [4][5]. The Apollo 15 and 16 instruments used a sodium iodide (NaI(Tl)) crystal with a plastic scintillator cover on a 7.6 metre boom [6]. The depth of material sampled by these instruments is not given in the sources read for this draft, so no sensing-depth figure is stated.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a lunar gamma-ray spectrometer is to map the chemical composition of the surface. The Lunar Prospector instrument was designed to map iron, titanium, uranium, thorium, potassium, silicon and oxygen, with magnesium, aluminium and calcium as objectives 'if possible' [2]. The Kaguya instrument was designed to determine the abundances of more than ten elements and to map hydrogen through its gamma-ray signature, supporting the search for water and studies of the Moon's origin and evolution [4]. Natural radioactivity from potassium, thorium and uranium is a central measurement, and the Apollo 15 and 16 instruments were primarily intended to study the Moon's radioactivity [6]. The Lunar Prospector GRS data are archived together with neutron spectrometer (NS) data in the PDS [3].
article.operating_principle: Galactic cosmic rays strike the lunar surface and produce neutrons in the subsurface. These neutrons interact with nuclei in the regolith and rock and release gamma rays with element-specific energies, and natural radioisotopes also emit gamma rays [4]. The detector records the energy of each arriving gamma ray. Pulse heights are sorted into energy channels to build a spectrum in which peaks identify elements and peak areas relate to abundance [2][4][5]. In a scintillator instrument, a gamma ray deposits energy in a crystal such as BGO, which emits light in proportion to that energy. A germanium semiconductor instead produces an electrical charge in proportion to the energy, and it must be cooled to operate, as the Kaguya team notes [4][5]. Because counting statistics need long integration times, the Lunar Prospector instrument recorded one spectrum every 32 seconds [1].
article.scientific_importance: Orbital gamma-ray spectrometry is one of the few ways to obtain global elemental maps of the Moon without landing. Lunar Prospector's instrument was designed to provide such maps for a set of major and trace-element targets [2]. Its calibrated data were migrated to the PDS4 standard in February 2021, so the global data are archived in a current format for reuse [3]. The Kaguya instrument's energy resolution was reported to be about 20 times better than that of earlier lunar missions, allowing finer discrimination between gamma-ray lines [4]. Together, the Apollo, Lunar Prospector and Kaguya measurements form a sequence of increasingly capable compositional datasets. The instruments differ in sensitivity, energy range and spatial resolution, so their outputs are not directly interchangeable [1][4][6].

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal specification for a gamma-ray detector. The three orbital examples and the planned rover example below use different crystals, shields, cooling systems and mounting arrangements. The values given apply only to the named instruments [1][4][5][6][7].

examples.name: Lunar Prospector Gamma-Ray Spectrometer (GRS)
examples.summary: This is the best-documented example in the sources read, because the PDS instrument catalogue gives its mass, power and crystal dimensions. The catalogue describes the instrument as designed to run continuously during the primary mission [1].
specs: Main detector: bismuth germanate (BGO) crystal, 7.1 cm diameter by 7.6 cm long [1]
Anticoincidence shield: borated plastic, 12 cm diameter by 20 cm long [1]
Mass: 8.6 kg [1]
Power: about 3 W [1]
Energy range: 0.3 to 9 MeV; energy sampling 17.6 keV [1]
Sensitivity: 2 to 8 times that of the Apollo gamma-ray spectrometer, varying with energy [1]
Spectrum acquisition: one spectrum every 32 seconds [1]
Mounting: on one of the spacecraft's three booms [1]
Thermal control: maintained at -28 °C for at least 1.5 years by a thermostat-controlled heater and thermal blanket [1]
Field of view: not stated in the source read [1]

examples.name: Kaguya (SELENE) Gamma Ray Spectrometer (GRS)
examples.summary: The Kaguya GRS was developed by a JAXA-led team, with Nobuyuki Hasebe listed as principal investigator on the JAXA mission page [4]. Its published physical specifications are incomplete in the sources read.
specs: Main detector: large germanium crystal; size not stated [5]
Anticoincidence detectors: a massive bismuth germanate crystal and a plastic scintillator [5]
Cooling: Stirling cryocooler; the detector is kept below -180 °C [4] and below 90 K during observation [5]
Energy range: 200 keV to 12 MeV [4][5]
Energy resolution: 3.0 keV FWHM at 1333 keV for the flight model [5]; JAXA reports resolution about 20 times better than earlier lunar missions [4]
Mass, power, dimensions and orbit altitude: not verified from the sources read [5]

examples.name: Apollo 15 and 16 command-module gamma-ray spectrometer
examples.type: Flown orbital lunar instrument (Apollo 15 and 16 command modules)
examples.summary: The Apollo 15 and 16 instruments were carried on the command modules and were primarily intended to study the Moon's radioactivity [6]. The sources read do not name the elements these instruments mapped, so no element list is stated here.
specs: Detector: 512-channel cylindrical sodium iodide NaI(Tl) scintillation spectrometer, 76 mm by 76 mm [6]
Shield: plastic scintillator cover that rejects charged particles [6]
Energy range: 0.55 to 8.6 MeV; energy resolution about 8% [6]
Mounting: on a 7.6 m boom [6]
Mass and power: not provided in the source read [6]

examples.name: Lunar-VISE Gamma Ray and Neutron Spectrometer (LV-GRNS)
examples.type: Planned rover-mounted instrument (NASA CLPS CP-21 delivery); no mission outcome verified
examples.summary: Included to show a surface-deployed approach. NASA's CP-21 description presents the delivery as planned, and no flight outcome was verified in this draft [7].
specs: Measurement: composition and abundances of lunar surface material [7]
Carrier: the Lunar-VISE payload suite is described as affixed to a rover and a lander; the LV-GRNS is carried on the rover, which the page does not name [7]
Mission: CP-21 on Firefly's Blue Ghost 3 lander, which the page says 'will deliver six NASA CLPS science payloads to the Gruithuisen Domes' [7]
Mass, power and other specifications: not stated [7]

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions differ widely between the examples. The Lunar Prospector sensor's crystal and shield are sized as a pair, with the borated-plastic shield larger than the crystal in both diameter and length [1]. The Apollo sensor is described as a 76 mm by 76 mm crystal [6]. Kaguya and LV-GRNS dimensions are not stated in the sources read [5][7]. No general dimension should be inferred for a new gamma-ray detector. As a general engineering note, the size depends on the crystal volume needed for counting statistics, the shield and the mounting.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The only documented instrument mass among the examples is the Lunar Prospector GRS at 8.6 kg [1]. The Apollo instrument mass is not provided in the source read [6], and the Kaguya GRS mass is not verified [5]. The LV-GRNS mass is not stated [7]. Mass drives launch and lander capacity, so each figure must be tied to a named instrument, and a new payload's mass would need a separate estimate.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The Lunar Prospector GRS is documented at about 3 W [1]. Power for the Apollo instrument and the Kaguya cryocooled germanium system is not stated in the sources read [5][6], and the LV-GRNS power is not stated [7]. The Kaguya team's use of a cryocooler means that cooling power is a real requirement, but no figure is given here [4][5].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar gamma-ray detector must survive the vacuum, radiation, micrometeoroid and temperature environment that affects other lunar instruments. The Lunar Prospector GRS was held at -28 °C by a heater and thermal blanket for at least 1.5 years [1], which shows that thermal control is a driving requirement. Germanium detectors need cryogenic cooling to operate [4][5], adding mass, power and mechanical complexity. Surface-deployed instruments must also cope with the lunar day-night cycle and with background from cosmic rays and from the host spacecraft or rover, which can contaminate spectra. These general engineering points are not tied to a specific instrument report in this draft.
article.limitations: Orbital gamma-ray spectrometers average over a footprint of surface material and over the upper layer of the regolith, so they cannot resolve fine-scale composition [2][4]. The sources read did not give the spatial resolution of any example, and the Kaguya page states none [4]. The sensitivity of the Lunar Prospector instrument varies with energy and is reported relative to Apollo, not as an absolute detection limit [1]. Germanium detectors need cryocooling, which constrains mass, power and lifetime [4][5]. Element lists in different sources do not always agree, so the element list for each instrument should be taken from its own mission documentation [2][6].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Gamma-ray spectrometers have reached the Moon as orbital instruments on lunar orbiters and command modules (Lunar Prospector, Kaguya, and the Apollo 15 and 16 command modules), and a surface instrument is planned for rover deployment (LV-GRNS) [1][4][6][7]. The surface case adds requirements that the orbital examples do not face.
transportation_process: Orbital case: integrate the spectrometer on the spacecraft, with the sensor on a boom or other mounting that keeps it away from the spacecraft background, as on Lunar Prospector and Apollo 15 and 16 [1][6].
Launch the spacecraft and place it in lunar orbit. The Kaguya mission was a lunar polar orbiter [5].
Commission the instrument, including cooling of any germanium detector to operating temperature before observations [4][5].
Surface case (planned): deliver the instrument on a lander with a rover, mount it on the rover and operate it as a rover payload, as described in the CP-21 plan [7].
Confirm power, data and thermal interfaces with the host spacecraft, rover or lander. No interface specification was verified in this draft.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Orbital instruments are fixed to the spacecraft, on a boom in the case of Lunar Prospector and Apollo 15 and 16 [1][6]. The planned LV-GRNS is carried on a rover [7]. How the rover deploys the instrument was not stated in the source read, so deployment details must be assessed against verified rover specifications.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 15 and 16 carried orbital gamma-ray spectrometers on their command modules [6]. Lunar Prospector's GRS flew on a NASA mission, and its calibrated data are archived by the PDS [1][3]. Kaguya carried the germanium-based GRS on the SELENE orbiter [4][5]. The LV-GRNS is a planned rover-mounted example [7].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with a specific lander or rover has not been verified for any gamma-ray detector in this draft. NASA's CP-21 description places the LV-GRNS on a rover delivered by Firefly's Blue Ghost 3 lander, but the page does not name the rover or give interface specifications [7]. Any new gamma-ray detector would need its mass, power, cryogenic requirements, mounting and thermal interfaces checked against verified spacecraft specifications.

article.historical_significance: Gamma-ray spectrometry of the Moon began in lunar orbit with the Apollo 15 and 16 instruments, which were primarily intended to study the Moon's radioactivity [6]. Lunar Prospector's GRS, with its BGO detector and calibrated data archived in the PDS, extended orbital elemental mapping, with objectives that included iron, titanium, uranium, thorium, potassium, silicon and oxygen [1][2][3]. The Kaguya GRS added a germanium detector with much finer energy resolution, and its objectives included mapping hydrogen as an indicator of water [4][5]. The planned LV-GRNS would take the technique to a rover [7].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The name 'gamma-ray detector' covers several instrument types, including scintillator spectrometers and germanium spectrometers, and some instruments combine gamma-ray and neutron sensing. Values for mass, power, dimensions and energy range are tied to named instruments and sources and must not be generalised [1][4][5][6][7]. Values not verified in this run include the Kaguya GRS mass, power and dimensions [5], the Apollo instrument mass and power [6], the LV-GRNS specifications [7], and the spatial resolution and sensing depth of each instrument. Secondary search summaries disagreed on the Lunar Prospector mission duration and on the coverage of the Apollo 15 and 16 maps, so neither figure is stated. The LV-GRNS status was verified only as far as NASA's CP-21 page, which describes the delivery as planned. No direct image asset was verified during this run, so the image registry is empty.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image assets were verified, so all image arrays are empty.

data_quality_notes: No image assets were verified or added. All image arrays are empty by design, and no image URL has been invented.
Kaguya GRS mass, power, dimensions and orbit altitude were not verified and are left unstated.
Apollo 15 and 16 element list and coverage were not verified in a primary source. Secondary summaries disagreed on coverage, so no percentage is stated.
Lunar Prospector mission duration was not verified in a primary source; secondary summaries disagreed (570 days versus 19 months), so no duration is stated.
LV-GRNS is described as planned in NASA's CP-21 page; no outcome was verified.
Spatial resolution and sensing depth were not verified for any instrument.
Web search used the payload name and technical keywords only. Secondary summaries were not used as citations; every citation is a page that was read.
